title: The Stripes That Moved the Continents
topic: seafloor magnetic stripes and the acceptance of plate tectonics
paragraphs: Few ideas in the Earth sciences have had a stranger career than continental drift.
In January 1912 the German meteorologist Alfred Wegener proposed that the continents had once been joined in a single landmass, which he later called Pangaea, and had since moved apart.
His book, The Origin of Continents and Oceans, appeared in 1915.

Wegener drew on several independent lines of evidence: the jigsaw fit of the South American and African coastlines, matching rock formations across the Atlantic, identical fossils on continents now an ocean apart, and signs of ancient glaciation in regions that today sit near the equator.
Any one of these could be explained away, but together they deserved a serious hearing.
They did not get one.

Wegener could describe what had happened but not how, and the mechanism he offered, continents plowing through the ocean floor under tidal forces and a push away from the poles, did not survive scrutiny.
The Cambridge geophysicist Harold Jeffreys showed that these forces were far too weak to move anything.
At a 1926 symposium in New York, American geologists lined up to reject the hypothesis, some in openly mocking terms.
Wegener died on the Greenland ice sheet in 1930, and for three decades drift was treated in most English-speaking departments as a cautionary tale.
In hindsight the reaction looks less like healthy caution than a refusal to take good evidence seriously because it lacked a tidy explanation.
The evidence that settled the matter came from the ocean floor, which in 1950 was almost entirely unmapped.
At the Lamont Geological Observatory in New York, Marie Tharp turned echo-sounding records into profiles of the Atlantic floor while Bruce Heezen collected the data at sea.

In 1952, plotting six profiles across the North Atlantic, Tharp noticed a deep notch at the crest of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge in every one and argued that it was a continuous rift valley down the center of the ridge.
Heezen at first dismissed the idea, but when earthquake epicenters from the ocean basins were plotted on the same map, they fell along the valley Tharp had drawn.
By 1957 the two had published a physiographic diagram of the North Atlantic floor, and later work traced the ridge and its rift around the globe as a mountain system roughly 65,000 kilometers long.
A rift valley is where crust is being pulled apart, and a rift that circles the planet is hard to reconcile with a static Earth.
Harry Hess of Princeton supplied the idea that gave the rift its meaning.
By 1960 he had collected several puzzles: the ocean floor carried only a thin blanket of sediment, nothing truly ancient had been recovered from it, and heat flow was unusually high at the ridges.

His answer, circulated in 1960 and published in 1962, was that mantle convection brings hot material up beneath the ridges, where it forms new floor that spreads outward in both directions and is eventually carried back into the mantle at the deep trenches.
Hess called his paper an essay in geopoetry, and Robert Dietz, publishing independently in 1961, gave the process its lasting name: seafloor spreading.
Spreading was still a hypothesis without a test, and the test came from an unlikely direction: the magnetism frozen into volcanic rock.
Basalt, the rock of the upper ocean crust, contains small grains of the iron oxide magnetite.
Above a threshold known as the Curie temperature, about 580 degrees Celsius for magnetite, the grains cannot hold a magnetic direction.
As a lava cools below that threshold, the grains lock in the direction and polarity of Earth's field at that moment, a property called thermoremanent magnetization.
Every basalt flow is therefore a compass reading taken on the day it solidified and kept ever since.
Those readings revealed something odd.

In 1906 the French physicist Bernard Brunhes reported lavas in central France magnetized roughly opposite to the present field, and in 1929 Motonori Matuyama showed that reversed lavas in Japan and Manchuria were consistently older than normal ones.
The obvious conclusion, that Earth's field flips its polarity from time to time, was resisted for decades.

In the early 1960s Allan Cox, Richard Doell and Brent Dalrymple of the United States Geological Survey paired magnetic measurements of lava flows with potassium-argon dating of the same flows and built a calendar of reversals.

They named the most recent intervals after pioneers of geomagnetism: the Brunhes normal epoch, in which we live, the Matuyama reversed epoch before it, then the Gauss normal and Gilbert reversed epochs.
The Brunhes-Matuyama boundary is now placed at about 780,000 years ago, and reversals proved to come irregularly, typically a few hundred thousand years apart.

In 1955 and 1956 a Coast and Geodetic Survey ship towing a magnetometer ran closely spaced lines off Washington, Oregon and California, and the map that Arthur Raff and Ronald Mason published in 1961 showed something nobody expected.
The field strength varied in long parallel bands, alternately slightly stronger and slightly weaker than the regional average, so that the floor looked striped like a zebra.
No one could say what had drawn the stripes.
The explanation arrived in September 1963 in a short paper in Nature by Fred Vine, a graduate student at Cambridge, and his supervisor Drummond Matthews.

New basalt at a ridge records the field of the day, and spreading carries each strip away from the axis in both directions, so the floor should be a tape recording of the reversal history: alternating bands symmetric about the ridge crest, normal bands adding to the present field and reversed bands subtracting from it.

Lawrence Morley of the Geological Survey of Canada had reached the same conclusion independently earlier that year, but Nature and then an American journal rejected his manuscript, one reviewer remarking that the idea belonged at a cocktail party rather than in print.
Even then, the reception was cool.
Lamont, which held an enormous archive of marine magnetic data, remained unconvinced.
Two developments in 1966 changed that.

First, Doell and Dalrymple identified a short normal interval inside the Matuyama epoch, the Jaramillo event, and once it was added to the calendar, seafloor profiles that had fit the model only roughly now fit it closely.

Second, in 1965 the research vessel Eltanin had crossed the Pacific-Antarctic Ridge on its nineteenth cruise towing a magnetometer, and when Walter Pitman and James Heirtzler plotted the profile, the anomalies on one side mirrored those on the other for hundreds of kilometers.
Folded about the ridge crest, the two halves of the Eltanin-19 profile matched peak for peak, and their spacing fit the reversal calendar if the floor spread at a few centimeters a year.
Shown at a conference in New York that November, the profile changed the minds of several prominent skeptics in the room.
Once the stripes were accepted, the rest followed fast.
The distance of a dated reversal from the ridge divided by its age gave a spreading rate, and the rates measured in ocean after ocean were slow, steady and sufficient to carry Wegener's continents.

In 1967 and 1968 Jason Morgan, Dan McKenzie and Robert Parker, and Xavier Le Pichon described Earth's surface as a small number of rigid plates moving over a sphere, and the theory acquired its modern name, plate tectonics.
Drilling by the Glomar Challenger in the South Atlantic in 1968 and 1969 then found sediment on the basalt growing older with distance from the ridge at very nearly the predicted rate.
The stripes are a direct physical record, written by the planet in its own rocks, of a process argued about for half a century.

The symmetry of the Eltanin-19 profile is, to my mind, among the most beautiful results in the Earth sciences: a single line of data that confirms spreading, reversals and drift at once, and that anyone can check with a ruler.
The rift valley was on Tharp's drafting table in 1952, Hess's essay was circulating in 1960, and the stripes were explained in 1963, yet most geologists did not come around until 1966 or later.
Caution has its place, but when the evidence is this clear, the delay says more about the habits of a profession than about the strength of the case.

questions.stem: According to the passage, which of the following was among the lines of evidence Wegener drew on for continental drift?
choices: The unusually high heat flow measured at the mid-ocean ridges
Signs of ancient glaciation in regions now near the equator
Earthquake epicenters lined up along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge
The thin blanket of sediment covering the ocean floor
Parallel magnetic stripes on the floor of the Pacific Ocean

proof.quote: signs of ancient glaciation in regions that today sit near the equator

questions.why: Paragraph 1 lists Wegener's evidence: the coastline fit, matching rocks, identical fossils, and signs of ancient glaciation in regions that now sit near the equator. The other choices are real details from the passage, but they belong to later discoveries by other people.
distractorNotes: Heat flow at the ridges is one of Hess's puzzles in paragraph 4, not part of Wegener's case.
The epicenters belong to Tharp and Heezen's rift valley in paragraph 3, decades after Wegener.
Thin sediment is a Hess puzzle from paragraph 4, not evidence Wegener used.
The stripes were found in the 1950s survey of paragraph 7; Wegener never saw them.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 1, the word 'hearing' most nearly means
choices: the physical sense by which sound is perceived
a formal proceeding before a judge
a fair chance to be considered
a lecture delivered to an audience
a rumor passed from person to person

proof.quote: together they deserved a serious hearing

questions.why: Paragraph 1 says the evidence 'deserved a serious hearing,' and paragraph 2 opens with 'They did not get one' and then describes geologists refusing the idea. So a hearing here is a fair chance to be considered, not the sense of hearing.
distractorNotes: That is the everyday meaning of the word, but a body of evidence cannot literally be listened to.
No court or judge appears anywhere in the passage; the hearing is figurative.
Wegener did give lectures, but the sentence is about how his evidence was received, not how it was delivered.
A rumor is unverified talk; the sentence is about evidence deserving serious consideration.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Harold Jeffreys's role in the debate over continental drift was to
choices: show that the forces Wegener proposed were far too weak
organize the 1926 symposium that rejected the hypothesis
propose that convection in the mantle could carry the continents
argue that the fossil evidence could be explained away
supply the mechanism that Wegener's proposal had lacked

proof.quote: showed that these forces were far too weak to move anything

questions.why: Paragraph 2 says Jeffreys 'showed that these forces were far too weak to move anything.' He attacked Wegener's mechanism; he did not provide one of his own.
distractorNotes: The passage names no organizer for the 1926 symposium and never places Jeffreys there.
Mantle convection is Hess's answer in paragraph 4, not anything Jeffreys proposed.
Paragraph 1 says any single line could be explained away, but that is the author's remark, not Jeffreys's argument.
Reversed: Jeffreys knocked down Wegener's mechanism rather than supplying a better one.

questions.stem: The author mentions earthquake epicenters in paragraph 3 primarily to
choices: explain why Tharp was not allowed to collect data at sea
suggest that the Mid-Atlantic Ridge is volcanically active
show that the ocean floor was almost entirely unmapped in 1950
show what persuaded Heezen that the rift valley was real
demonstrate that the ridge system is 65,000 kilometers long

proof.quote: they fell along the valley Tharp had drawn

questions.why: Paragraph 3 says Heezen 'at first dismissed the idea, but when earthquake epicenters from the ocean basins were plotted on the same map, they fell along the valley Tharp had drawn.' The epicenters are there to show what changed his mind.
distractorNotes: The passage never says why Tharp stayed ashore; it only says Heezen collected the data at sea.
Volcanic activity is not mentioned in paragraph 3; the epicenters tie to the rift, not to volcanoes.
The unmapped floor is the paragraph's opening claim and has nothing to do with the epicenters.
The length of the ridge comes from later work in the next sentence, not from the epicenters.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the mid-ocean ridge and its central rift
choices: were first noticed during the Eltanin's nineteenth cruise
form a mountain system roughly 65,000 kilometers long
were discovered by Harry Hess using a naval echo sounder
appear only in the six profiles Tharp plotted in 1952
were mapped completely before the Second World War

proof.quote: a mountain system roughly 65,000 kilometers long

questions.why: Paragraph 3 says later work 'traced the ridge and its rift around the globe as a mountain system roughly 65,000 kilometers long.'
distractorNotes: The Eltanin crossed the Pacific-Antarctic Ridge in 1965 (paragraph 9); the rift was recognized in 1952.
Hess supplied the idea that explained the rift (paragraph 4); Tharp and Heezen found it, and no echo sounder is tied to Hess.
Too narrow: the rift showed in all six profiles and was later traced around the globe.
Reversed: paragraph 3 says the floor was almost entirely unmapped in 1950.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that Hess's hypothesis accounted for the thin blanket of sediment on the ocean floor because
choices: the deep trenches swallow sediment faster than it accumulates
the high heat flow at the ridges bakes the sediment away
the sediment settles mainly on the continents instead
the floor is continually renewed and so is never very old
Dietz had already shown that the sediment was thin in 1961

proof.quote: nothing truly ancient had been recovered from it
it forms new floor that spreads outward in both directions and is eventually carried back into the mantle at the deep trenches

questions.why: Paragraph 4 pairs the puzzles (thin sediment, nothing ancient) with Hess's answer: new floor forms at the ridges and is carried back into the mantle at the trenches. If the floor is constantly made and destroyed it is young, and young floor has had little time to collect sediment.
distractorNotes: The passage says the floor itself is carried into the trenches; it never says trenches remove sediment faster than it forms.
Heat flow is listed as a puzzle, not as a process that destroys sediment.
Nothing in the passage says sediment settles on the continents.
Dietz is credited with the name seafloor spreading, not with any measurement of sediment.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 4, all of the following are true of Hess's proposal EXCEPT:
choices: It was circulated in 1960, two years before it was published.
It invoked mantle convection beneath the mid-ocean ridges.
It had new floor carried back into the mantle at the trenches.
Hess himself described the paper as an essay in geopoetry.
Hess gave the process its lasting name, seafloor spreading.

proof.quote: circulated in 1960 and published in 1962
mantle convection brings hot material up beneath the ridges
carried back into the mantle at the deep trenches
Hess called his paper an essay in geopoetry
Robert Dietz, publishing independently in 1961, gave the process its lasting name: seafloor spreading

questions.why: Four choices come straight from paragraph 4. Its last sentence says it was Robert Dietz, not Hess, who gave the process the name seafloor spreading.
distractorNotes: Stated in paragraph 4: 'circulated in 1960 and published in 1962.'
Stated in paragraph 4: 'mantle convection brings hot material up beneath the ridges.'
Stated in paragraph 4: new floor is 'eventually carried back into the mantle at the deep trenches.'
Stated in paragraph 4: 'Hess called his paper an essay in geopoetry.'

questions.stem: According to the passage, the Curie temperature is the temperature
choices: at which basalt begins to melt into lava
at which Earth's magnetic field reverses its polarity
above which magnetite grains cannot hold a magnetic direction
below which potassium-argon dating of a lava flow becomes unreliable
at which hot material begins to rise beneath the ridges

proof.quote: the grains cannot hold a magnetic direction

questions.why: Paragraph 5 defines it directly: above the Curie temperature, about 580 degrees Celsius for magnetite, 'the grains cannot hold a magnetic direction.'
distractorNotes: Melting is never mentioned; the Curie temperature is about magnetism, not melting.
Reversals are a behavior of Earth's field (paragraph 6), not a temperature.
Potassium-argon dating appears in paragraph 6 with no temperature attached to it.
That describes mantle convection from paragraph 4, not the Curie temperature.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that if an ancient basalt flow were reheated well above 580 degrees Celsius and then allowed to cool again, it would
choices: record the field as it was at the time of the reheating
preserve its original compass reading unchanged
lose its magnetite grains entirely
record both the original and the new field at once
become impossible to date by the potassium-argon dating method

proof.quote: the grains cannot hold a magnetic direction
lock in the direction and polarity of Earth's field at that moment

questions.why: Paragraph 5 says that above the Curie temperature the grains cannot hold a direction, and that on cooling below it they lock in the field 'at that moment.' Reheating erases the old reading; cooling again writes a new one.
distractorNotes: Reversed: above the Curie temperature the grains cannot hold a direction, so the old reading is lost.
The passage says the grains lose their magnetic direction, not that they disappear.
The grains lock in the field 'at that moment,' a single reading, not two.
Nothing in the passage links the Curie temperature to potassium-argon dating.

questions.stem: According to the passage, Cox, Doell and Dalrymple built their calendar of reversals by
choices: towing a magnetometer behind a research vessel across the Pacific-Antarctic Ridge
comparing the lavas of central France with those of Japan and Manchuria
folding seafloor magnetic profiles about the crest of the ridge
pairing magnetic measurements of lava flows with potassium-argon dates
drilling into the sediment that rests on the basalt of the South Atlantic

proof.quote: paired magnetic measurements of lava flows with potassium-argon dating of the same flows

questions.why: Paragraph 6 says they 'paired magnetic measurements of lava flows with potassium-argon dating of the same flows and built a calendar of reversals.'
distractorNotes: That is the Eltanin survey in paragraph 9, worked up by Pitman and Heirtzler.
Brunhes and Matuyama studied those lavas decades earlier; the calendar came from dated flows.
Folding the profile is what revealed the Eltanin-19 symmetry in paragraph 9.
Drilling is the Glomar Challenger work described in paragraph 10.

questions.stem: According to the passage, all of the following are true of geomagnetic reversals EXCEPT:
choices: Brunhes reported reversely magnetized lavas in France in 1906.
Matuyama found that reversed lavas were older than normal ones.
The idea that the field flips was resisted for decades.
The Brunhes-Matuyama boundary is now placed near 780,000 years ago.
Reversals recur at a regular interval of about 780,000 years.

proof.quote: In 1906 the French physicist Bernard Brunhes reported lavas in central France magnetized roughly opposite to the present field
reversed lavas in Japan and Manchuria were consistently older than normal ones
was resisted for decades
now placed at about 780,000 years ago
reversals proved to come irregularly, typically a few hundred thousand years apart

questions.why: Paragraph 6 confirms the other four choices. Its last sentence says reversals 'come irregularly, typically a few hundred thousand years apart,' so a fixed 780,000-year interval is contradicted; 780,000 years is the age of one boundary, not a repeating period.
distractorNotes: Stated in paragraph 6: Brunhes, 1906, lavas in central France magnetized opposite to the present field.
Stated in paragraph 6: reversed lavas in Japan and Manchuria were 'consistently older than normal ones.'
Stated in paragraph 6: the conclusion 'was resisted for decades.'
Stated in paragraph 6: the boundary is 'now placed at about 780,000 years ago.'

questions.stem: The author describes Lawrence Morley's experience in paragraph 8 primarily to
choices: suggest that Vine and Matthews had taken the idea from his rejected manuscript
explain why Nature was the most prestigious journal in the field
show that the magnetic stripes were first discovered in Canada
illustrate how unwelcome the idea was even when it was right
argue that cocktail parties are where good science is first discussed

proof.quote: one reviewer remarking that the idea belonged at a cocktail party rather than in print

questions.why: Paragraph 8 says Morley reached the same conclusion independently, yet two journals rejected it and a reviewer mocked it. The episode shows the field dismissing a correct idea, which feeds the author's larger point about slow acceptance.
distractorNotes: The passage says Morley reached the conclusion 'independently,' which is the opposite of anyone borrowing it.
Nothing is said about Nature's prestige; it is simply where the Vine and Matthews paper appeared.
The stripes were found off Washington, Oregon and California (paragraph 7), not in Canada.
The cocktail party remark was a reviewer's insult, not a recommendation from the author.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that a band of seafloor where the measured field is slightly stronger than the regional average most likely
choices: formed when the field had the same polarity as today
lies directly beneath the crest of the mid-ocean ridge
is older than the reversed bands on either side of it
contains more magnetite than the neighboring bands
formed during the Matuyama reversed epoch

proof.quote: normal bands adding to the present field and reversed bands subtracting from it

questions.why: Paragraph 8 explains that normal bands add to the present field and reversed bands subtract from it. A slightly stronger reading therefore marks floor that cooled when the field pointed the way it does now.
distractorNotes: Position relative to the crest tells you age, not polarity; stronger bands occur at many distances from it.
Age depends on distance from the ridge (paragraph 10), not on polarity; one neighbor is older and one is younger.
The passage ties the stripes to polarity, not to how much magnetite a band contains.
Reversed: the Matuyama epoch was reversed, and a reversed band subtracts from the present field.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the Eltanin-19 profile was striking because
choices: it was the first magnetic survey ever run across an ocean ridge
it revealed the Jaramillo event for the first time
it showed the ocean floor spreading far faster than anyone had believed possible
it was gathered off the Pacific coast of North America
its anomalies on one side of the ridge mirrored those on the other

proof.quote: the anomalies on one side mirrored those on the other for hundreds of kilometers

questions.why: Paragraph 9 says that when Pitman and Heirtzler plotted the profile, 'the anomalies on one side mirrored those on the other for hundreds of kilometers,' and that folded about the crest the two halves matched peak for peak.
distractorNotes: The passage never calls it the first; an earlier magnetometer survey appears in paragraph 7.
Doell and Dalrymple identified the Jaramillo event from lava flows, not from this profile.
The passage gives a rate of a few centimeters a year and calls spreading slow and steady (paragraph 10).
That is the Raff and Mason survey of paragraph 7; the Eltanin crossed the Pacific-Antarctic Ridge.

questions.stem: Which of the following best illustrates the principle described in paragraph 5?
choices: A compass needle continuously swings to follow the field wherever it is carried
Wet cement poured over a leaf hardens and keeps the leaf's imprint for decades
A thermometer on a wall rises and falls with the temperature of the room
Iron filings line up along the field lines when a magnet is held beneath the paper
A weather vane turns to point into whatever wind is blowing at the moment

proof.quote: the grains lock in the direction and polarity of Earth's field at that moment
a compass reading taken on the day it solidified and kept ever since

questions.why: Paragraph 5's principle is that a material locks in a record of conditions at the moment it solidifies and keeps that record afterward. Cement hardening around a leaf does exactly that; the other cases respond to present conditions and keep no record.
distractorNotes: A compass tracks the current field and keeps no record, the opposite of locking in a reading.
A thermometer responds to the present temperature and remembers nothing once it changes.
Filings show the field at this moment; move the magnet and the pattern changes with it.
A weather vane follows the present wind and keeps no record of past winds.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the geological profession's handling of continental drift is best described as
choices: unreserved admiration
puzzled curiosity
measured criticism
bitter contempt
complete indifference

proof.quote: a refusal to take good evidence seriously because it lacked a tidy explanation
the delay says more about the habits of a profession than about the strength of the case

questions.why: The judging words are in paragraph 2 ('less like healthy caution than a refusal to take good evidence seriously') and paragraph 11 ('says more about the habits of a profession'). The author faults the delay but grants that 'caution has its place,' so the criticism is measured rather than bitter.
distractorNotes: Admiration is reserved for the evidence, especially the Eltanin-19 profile, not for the profession's response.
The author is not puzzled; the delay is explained as a habit of the profession.
Too strong: 'caution has its place' and the respectful account of the scientists rule out contempt.
The author plainly cares, calling the evidence beautiful and the delay telling.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?
choices: Seafloor magnetic stripes supplied the evidence that turned continental drift into plate tectonics
Alfred Wegener was the first scientist to propose that the continents had once been joined
Marie Tharp's discovery of the rift valley was unfairly credited to Bruce Heezen
Earth's magnetic field reverses its polarity at irregular intervals of a few hundred thousand years
The symmetric Eltanin-19 profile was the single piece of evidence that persuaded geologists to accept seafloor spreading

proof.quote: the test came from an unlikely direction: the magnetism frozen into volcanic rock
the floor should be a tape recording of the reversal history
The stripes are a direct physical record, written by the planet in its own rocks, of a process argued about for half a century
a single line of data that confirms spreading, reversals and drift at once

questions.why: The passage opens with drift rejected for lack of a mechanism, then builds to the magnetic test (paragraph 5), the stripe prediction (paragraph 8) and the author's verdict in paragraph 11 that the stripes are the record that settled the argument. The answer covers that whole arc.
distractorNotes: True, but it is only paragraph 1; the passage is about how drift was finally proven.
The passage never says credit was taken from Tharp; it says Heezen was at first unconvinced.
A detail from paragraph 6, one piece of the story rather than its point.
Too strong: the Jaramillo event and the Glomar Challenger drilling also mattered.
